content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Epidemiological profile of HPV infection, associations with cervical lesions and vaginal microecological disorders, and nine-valent vaccine coverage in Northwest China: a 6-year retrospective study of 57,035 women by October 21, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Epidemiological profile of HPV infection, associations with cervical lesions and vaginal microecological disorders, and nine-valent vaccine coverage in Northwest China: a 6-year retrospective study of 57,035 women Check Symptoms Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A six-year retrospective study of 57,035 female outpatients at a tertiary hospital in Shaanxi Province found that 28.77% were positive for human papillomavirus (HPV), with isolated high-risk HPV infections and single-genotype patterns dominating the results. The analysis, reported in Virology Journal, also examined persistent infections, associations between particular HPV genotypes and cervical lesions, relationships with vaginal microecological disorders, and the prevalence of genotypes covered by the nine-valent HPV vaccine. The hospital-based study included female outpatients who underwent HPV genotyping from 2016 through 2021. HPV prevalence followed a bimodal age distribution, reaching its highest level among participants aged 26–30 years and showing a secondary peak among those aged 61 years or older. HPV16 was the most prevalent high-risk genotype, followed by HPV52, HPV58, HPV53 and HPV51. Because the study recruited patients at one tertiary hospital, the findings characterize the women included in the clinical sample rather than establishing population-representative HPV prevalence across Northwest China. Discover more Track Outbreaks Track Fertility Study Anatomy Persistent infection was assessed in 3,542 patients who returned for follow-up. Of these, 33.75% had persistent HPV infection, with the highest persistence rate recorded among people with mixed high-risk and low-risk HPV infections. HPV positivity was correlated with elevated abnormal rates on thin-prep cytology tests, and nine high-risk HPV genotypes were significantly associated with cytological abnormalities. In the cervical cancer cases included in the analysis, HPV16 accounted for 69.7%. These findings describe statistical associations in the retrospective cohort; they do not establish that a particular HPV genotype caused an individual cervical lesion or cancer. Check Symptoms Discover more Book a Checkup Find Vaccines vaccine Donate to Research The study also evaluated associations between HPV infection and bacterial vaginosis, aerobic vaginitis, trichomonal vaginitis, vulvovaginal candidiasis and mixed vaginitis. HPV positivity was positively associated with bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and mixed vaginitis but inversely associated with vulvovaginal candidiasis. The strength and direction of these relationships varied by HPV subtype, indicating that the results differed among viral types. The supplied findings document associations within the analyzed patients and do not show that HPV caused a vaginal disorder or that any vaginal disorder increased HPV risk. Similarly, the reported increase in the proportion of nine-valent-vaccine-covered genotypes with increasing cervical lesion severity describes the distribution of viral genotypes in the cohort, not vaccination uptake or the vaccine’s protective effect. content: Creative Diagnostics Introduces High-Risk HPV L1 Virus-Like Particles Produced in Yeast for Research and Assay Development Creative Diagnostics launches a range of High-Risk HPV L1 VLPs Produced in Yeast to support HPV research applications. New York, NY, United States - October 23, 2026 - Creative Diagnostics, a leading manufacturer and supplier of antibodies, antigens and assay kits, has launched a range of High-Risk HPV L1 VLPs Produced in Yeast [https://www.creative-diagnostics.com/high-risk-hpv-l1-vlps-produced-in-yeast.htm], a portfolio of recombinant virus-like particle (VLP) antigens to support human papillomavirus (HPV) research, serological assay development, antibody evaluation, and vaccine-related investigations. This new product line provides researchers and laboratory professionals with access to L1 VLP antigens that represent multiple high-risk HPV genotypes, which can help to advance studies of HPV-specific immune responses and antigen recognition. HPV is a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus with a T=7 icosahedral capsid composed of 72 L1 pentamers (capsomeres), which are paired with L2 monomers. The L1 and L2 proteins have similar molecular weights (approximately 55kDa), with minor differences among different HPV genotypes. HPV has evolved a highly refined infection mechanism and exhibits specificity regarding the species, tissues and cell types it infects. Furthermore, the HPV virion enters the host via routes other than body fluids, resulting in a weak immune response from the host against neutralizing epitopes on the capsid. Given this low immune pressure, as well as the fact that the human antiviral immune response is primarily driven by type-specific neutralization, the HPV phylogeny is highly complex, with more than 200 distinct genotypes having accumulated to date. As there is currently no efficient method of extracting natural antigens from cultures, serological testing for HPV relies primarily on the use of "virus-like particles" (VLPs). When expressed via recombinant technology, the major HPV capsid protein L1 self-assembles into VLPs. These VLPs do not contain the viral genome, but they present type-specific conformational epitopes that are similar to those found in real viral particles. HPV L1 VLPs can induce high-titre, type-specific neutralizing antibodies and form the basis of current preventive vaccines. To better support scientific research in HPV immunology and diagnostics, Creative Diagnostics now provides researchers with high-risk HPV L1 VLPs produced in yeast, which are ideal for HPV-related research, diagnostic reagent development, antibody evaluation and viral antigen characterization. These antigens are based on the major capsid protein L1 of clinically significant high-risk HPV types. When properly expressed and processed, the L1 protein self-assembles into VLPs that resemble natural HPV capsids in structure but do not contain viral genomic material. This makes L1 VLPs non-infectious antigenic reagents that are particularly suitable for research that require the presentation of a natural capsid structure. Creative Diagnostics' new product portfolio covers nine high-risk genotypes relevant to cervical cancer research, HPV epidemiology, and immune response profiling, including HPV16, HPV18, HPV31, HPV33, HPV35, HPV45, HPV52, HPV59 and HPV68. This comprehensive testing panel enables the parallel comparison of subtype-specific antibody responses, cross-reactivity and antigenic performance across multiple high-risk genotypes. For researchers and assay developers who are interested in evaluating the High-Risk HPV L1 VLPs portfolio, product specifications, availability, application-specific requirements , or requesting bulk production, please visit https://www.creative-diagnostics.com/high-risk-hpv-l1-vlps-produced-in-yeast.htm. About Creative Diagnostics Creative Diagnostics is a leading manufacturer and supplier of antibodies, viral antigens, innovative diagnostic components, and critical assay reagents. In addition to providing contract R&D and biologic manufacturing services for diagnostic manufacturers along with GMP biologics manufacturing for the biopharmaceutical market, the company aims to continue to act as a trusted source for all researchers' assay development and manufacturing needs. content_title: JVI|科学家在野生型HPV18中发现能够提升病毒稳定性和感染性的新型 L1蛋白
content: 顶部 首页 首页 雾 / 10° 隐私 JVI|科学家在野生型HPV18中发现能够提升病毒稳定性和感染性的新型 L1蛋白 病毒学界 深入探索 考研辅导 体验极速搜索 登录服务 前期研究通常认为,人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)衣壳蛋白病毒颗粒仅含有L1一种形式构成,现有疫苗、假病毒、类病毒颗粒等实验材料大多依靠许多HPV亚型中都存在的共有甲硫氨酸序列的L1重组表达载体系统制备。然而,HPV18的L1蛋白在共有甲硫氨酸序列上游的61位和26位氨基酸位置上,分别含有两个额外的连续甲硫氨酸残基,这些残基被排除在用于合成重组病毒的L1表达载体之外。近期,来自美国的科学家发现,HPV18的L1蛋白61位氨基酸位置上的连续甲硫氨酸残基,对于病毒的稳定性和感染性至关重要,去除该残疾可导致L1的衣壳蛋白的构象发生改变,并显著降低HPV18的稳定性和感染性。该研究成果目前已发表至Journal of Virology杂志,题为‘New form of HPV18 L1 found in native virions contributes to virion stability and infectivity’。 研究人员通过构建器官型筏式培养获得原始HPV18病毒,发现野生型 HPV18 病毒能够表达两种不同的L1异构体,其中一种较长的异构体是从上游的甲硫氨酸翻译而来的。证实野生型HPV18可利用上游M (−61)翻译产生N端延长的长型L1,同时利用保守M (1)翻译短型L1,两种L1亚型均可组装进成熟病毒颗粒,M (−26)不参与功能性L1合成。敲除M(−61)后,病毒仅表达短L1,衣壳构象发生改变,病毒颗粒稳定性显著下降,对消毒剂更敏感,感染能力下降超过50%。 展开剩余 31 % 该研究颠覆HPV衣壳蛋白仅含单一L1亚型的传统认知,揭示天然HPV18病毒颗粒存在两种L1蛋白异构体。现有重组VLPs、假病毒缺少M(−61)编码的N端延伸L1序列,与真实天然病毒存在结构、稳定性差异。该发现更新了HPV衣壳蛋白生物学认知,对HPV疫苗研发、诊断试剂开发、抗病毒药物、病毒灭活消毒策略制定具有重要参考价值,同时提示其他部分高危HPV亚型也可能存在类似的非经典翻译起始机制,为后续病毒翻译调控、病毒颗粒改造提供新研究方向。 Free web novels for online reading. 深入探索 发现精彩活动 参与公益活动 娱乐新闻 评论 全部 还没有人评论过,快来抢首评 抢首评 推荐阅读 刘欢走了才敢说!杀死他的不是股骨头坏死,而是明知不可为而为之 司徒夜 昨天08:49 18.7万+ 车模小姐姐太会啦!这格纹短裙配披肩,谁看了不迷糊? content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Retrospective blood protein models predict outcomes in 38 HPV16 cancer patients by October 21, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Retrospective blood protein models predict outcomes in 38 HPV16 cancer patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Serum protein measurements collected before treatment or early during therapy predicted clinical benefit and overall survival in 38 patients with advanced HPV16-positive malignancies receiving a three-drug combination immunotherapy, according to a retrospective analysis of a clinical trial. Models using baseline concentrations of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and heme oxygenase 1, alone or together with an early change in granzyme B, identified patient groups more likely to benefit from treatment and to have longer overall survival. Because the findings come from retrospective data, the researchers said the models require prospective validation before they can be evaluated as clinical prediction tools. The trial regimen combined PDS0101, an HPV16 therapeutic peptide cancer vaccine intended to initiate an immune response; PDS01ADC, a tumor-targeting interleukin-12 immunocytokine intended to potentiate that response; and bintrafusp alfa, a bifunctional agent designed to block both programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta). A prior report from trial NCT04287868 described promising clinical activity in patients with advanced HPV16-associated malignancies. The updated analysis examined peripheral immune and serum proteomic measurements in an attempt to identify correlates of clinical response to the combination. For the proteomic analysis, the investigators surveyed serum proteins and built machine-learning models using data available before therapy or early in the regimen. The reported predictive signals were baseline IL-6 and heme oxygenase 1 concentrations, either used alone or combined with an early change in granzyme B. These models were designed to predict both clinical benefit and the duration of overall survival. Their results show that molecular patterns measured in blood contained outcome-related information in this cohort, but they do not establish that the proteins caused the observed differences in response or survival. Discover more Find Cancer Care Cancer cancer Study Biology Book Care Services The researchers also conducted a broader survey of the peripheral immunome. Among patients who benefited from treatment, they identified a persistent skewing toward increased ratios of peripheral CD8-positive T cells to myeloid cells. The analysis did not determine whether this cellular pattern produced the better outcomes. It also found a positive association between the frequencies of monocytes and myeloid-derived suppressor cells and serum concentrations of inhibitory biomarkers. According to the authors, that association supplies biological context for the serum-based prediction models by linking measurements of particular circulating cell populations with inhibitory molecular signals. These findings come from a retrospective study in a cohort of 38 patients with HPV16-positive tumors, and the investigators explicitly called for prospective validation in future clinical studies. The scope of the work was therefore outcome prediction within an already treated trial population, rather than a prospective test of whether clinicians could use serum measurements to select treatment or estimate an individual patient’s survival. The study instead supports further evaluation of minimally invasive molecular measurements obtained before or early in the regimen. Whether the models retain their predictive performance in independent prospective cohorts remains to be determined. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Retrospective blood protein models predict outcomes in 38 HPV16 cancer patients by October 21, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Retrospective blood protein models predict outcomes in 38 HPV16 cancer patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Serum protein measurements collected before treatment or early during therapy predicted clinical benefit and overall survival in 38 patients with advanced HPV16-positive malignancies receiving a three-drug combination immunotherapy, according to a retrospective analysis of a clinical trial. Models using baseline concentrations of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and heme oxygenase 1, alone or together with an early change in granzyme B, identified patient groups more likely to benefit from treatment and to have longer overall survival. Because the findings come from retrospective data, the researchers said the models require prospective validation before they can be evaluated as clinical prediction tools. The trial regimen combined PDS0101, an HPV16 therapeutic peptide cancer vaccine intended to initiate an immune response; PDS01ADC, a tumor-targeting interleukin-12 immunocytokine intended to potentiate that response; and bintrafusp alfa, a bifunctional agent designed to block both programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta). A prior report from trial NCT04287868 described promising clinical activity in patients with advanced HPV16-associated malignancies. The updated analysis examined peripheral immune and serum proteomic measurements in an attempt to identify correlates of clinical response to the combination. For the proteomic analysis, the investigators surveyed serum proteins and built machine-learning models using data available before therapy or early in the regimen. The reported predictive signals were baseline IL-6 and heme oxygenase 1 concentrations, either used alone or combined with an early change in granzyme B. These models were designed to predict both clinical benefit and the duration of overall survival. Their results show that molecular patterns measured in blood contained outcome-related information in this cohort, but they do not establish that the proteins caused the observed differences in response or survival. The researchers also conducted a broader survey of the peripheral immunome. Among patients who benefited from treatment, they identified a persistent skewing toward increased ratios of peripheral CD8-positive T cells to myeloid cells. The analysis did not determine whether this cellular pattern produced the better outcomes. It also found a positive association between the frequencies of monocytes and myeloid-derived suppressor cells and serum concentrations of inhibitory biomarkers. According to the authors, that association supplies biological context for the serum-based prediction models by linking measurements of particular circulating cell populations with inhibitory molecular signals. These findings come from a retrospective study in a cohort of 38 patients with HPV16-positive tumors, and the investigators explicitly called for prospective validation in future clinical studies. The scope of the work was therefore outcome prediction within an already treated trial population, rather than a prospective test of whether clinicians could use serum measurements to select treatment or estimate an individual patient’s survival. The study instead supports further evaluation of minimally invasive molecular measurements obtained before or early in the regimen. Whether the models retain their predictive performance in independent prospective cohorts remains to be determined. Children are more likely to be fully vaccinated against HPV—a ubiquitous virus that causes six types of cancer— if doctors offer the immunization when kids are 9 or 10 years old, compared with beginning the series of injections at ages 11 or 12, the age when most clinicians now offer the shots. That’s according to a study presented at IDWeek, a major infectious disease conference in Washington, DC. By age 13, more than 77% of children in the study who were offered an HPV vaccination at the younger age received at least one dose, and 62% had received both shots, compared with 67% and 45% of kids, respectively, offered the immunization at the older age. Overall, children offered the HPV shot earlier were more than twice as likely to begin vaccination, as well as complete the two-dose HPV vaccine series, compared with kids offered the immunization at the older age, according to the study, which included 31 pediatric practices in Colorado and California from 2021 to 2026. The median age at which youngsters completed the two-dose series was 12.2 years among those offered vaccination at an earlier age, compared with 13.3 years among those offered the shots later. “Parental concerns, pushback, hesitancy, and acceptance didn't really seem to differ between the groups,” said Sean O’Leary, MD, MPH, first author of the study and a professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine, at a press briefing before the conference. “Most parents were receptive to the change.” HPV uptake in US teens has stagnated Most parents seemed comfortable with vaccinating their children earlier, O’Leary said. In interviews, clinicians said that their conversations with families were shorter when they offered vaccination at an earlier age, said O’Leary, director of the Colorado Children’s Outcomes Network, a practice-based research network. FatCamera / iStock The main objection to vaccinating against HPV at ages 9 or 10 came from parents who had told their children that there would be no shots during this visit. Parents “wanted warnings upfront,” in order to better prepare their children, O’Leary said. Doctors have been looking for ways to increase HPV vaccination. Although two decades of research show the vaccine is safe, coverage rates among teens have stagnated. Research by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) finds that 78.2% of teens ages 13 to 17 received one or more doses of the HPV vaccine from 2022 to 2024, with 62.9% reporting they had received both recommended doses. Most parents were receptive to the change. The World Health Organization’s blueprint for eliminating cervical cancer—which is almost always caused by HPV—calls for fully vaccinating 90% of girls against HPV by age 15. HPV also causes cancer in men, including tumors of the throat, penis, and anus. Earlier shot shifts timing, boosts overall coverage The new study answers an important question, said Kengo Inagaki, MD, vice chair of IDWeek for the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society, who was not involved in the new research. Pediatricians have wondered if starting the HPV series at 9 years old would improve overall coverage, or simply shift vaccination to a younger age, said Inagaki, director of the pediatric transplant infectious diseases program at the University of Michigan C.S. Mott Children’s Hospital. “By doing this randomized trial, investigators were able to prove that early initiation of vaccination does both of these things,” Inagaki said. “It shifts the timing of vaccination and also increases the overall coverage.” Studies show that HPV vaccines are most effective if provided before people are exposed to HPV through sexual contact, Inagaki said. Flexibility on timing Currently, parents and healthcare providers have flexibility about timing HPV vaccinations. The American Academy of Pediatrics and American Cancer Society recommend boys and girls receive the first of two doses of HPV vaccine from ages 9 to 12. The CDC currently allows kids to be vaccinated as early as 9 years old, but it recommends beginning the two-dose vaccine series at ages 11 or 12, when kids receive two other vaccines and when clinicians address a number of preteen health issues. Offering HPV vaccines earlier allows children to receive fewer shots in one visit, O’Leary said. And children in the study who were vaccinated against HPV at younger ages were just as likely as older children to receive other childhood immunizations on time, O’Leary said. Questions about length of efficacy Children vaccinated against HPV at age 9 show a robust immune response that lasts at least 15 years, O’Leary said. The HPV shot has been available for just 20 years, so the data on long-term efficacy are limited. But studies show that HPV vaccination spurs the body to produce a lot of antibodies against the virus right away, O’Leary said. As time goes by, the number of antibodies falls but remains high. Early vaccination may more effectively frame HPV vaccine as cancer prevention, not necessarily a conversation about sexuality. “The hope is that the vaccine efficacy will last for a long period of time, potentially covering adulthood, but we don’t yet have data to support that,” Inagaki said. Some parents have been reluctant to vaccinate their children against HPV, because they don’t want to appear to condone premarital sex. There’s no evidence, however, that people vaccinated against HPV become sexually active at earlier ages. In fact, sexual activity among teens has decreased since the vaccine was released. “Early vaccination may more effectively frame HPV vaccine as cancer prevention, not necessarily a conversation about sexuality,” O’Leary said. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Retrospective cohort links age, HPV type to persistence in women with cervical LSIL by October 22, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Retrospective cohort links age, HPV type to persistence in women with cervical LSIL Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a retrospective cohort study of 3,563 women with cervical low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection was independently associated with older age, infection with HPV-52 or HPV-58, and infection with multiple high-risk HPV types. The study, conducted at Guangdong Women and Children Hospital in Guangzhou from January 2021 through August 2025, also found that bacterial vaginosis, intermediate bacterial vaginosis and vulvovaginal candidiasis were inversely associated with persistent infection. These observations represent statistical associations from retrospective data and do not establish that the factors cause infection to persist. Researchers classified participants as persistently infected when the same high-risk HPV subtype was detected for at least 365 days, a group that included 919 women. The remaining 2,644 women were classified as having transient infection, defined as detection for more than 30 but fewer than 365 days. All participants underwent vaginal microecological testing, HPV genotyping and cervical cytology concurrently. The investigators used multivariable logistic regression to identify factors independently associated with persistent high-risk HPV infection, reporting odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals and P values. Age was associated with persistence in five-year increments: each additional five years corresponded to an odds ratio of 1.13, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.09 to 1.17 and P<0.001. HPV-52 and HPV-58 infection together were associated with higher odds of persistence, with an odds ratio of 1.65 (95% CI 1.38–1.98; P<0.001). Multiple high-risk HPV infections were also associated with persistence, producing an odds ratio of 1.50 (95% CI 1.24–1.81; P<0.001). By contrast, bacterial vaginosis was associated with lower odds of persistent high-risk HPV infection, with an odds ratio of 0.69 (95% CI 0.55–0.88; P=0.002), as was intermediate bacterial vaginosis at 0.66 (95% CI 0.52–0.84; P<0.001). Vulvovaginal candidiasis had an odds ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.58–0.96; P=0.024) in the adjusted analysis. The study also assessed recurrence burden for aerobic vaginitis, bacterial vaginosis and vulvovaginal candidiasis using negative binomial regression, with recurrence expressed as an incidence density per 100 person-years. Among women with persistent high-risk HPV infection, aerobic vaginitis had the highest measured recurrence burden, estimated at 35.77 episodes per 100 person-years (95% CI 33.17–38.53). The supplied research report states that this burden exceeded the burdens of the other vaginal conditions evaluated, although the complete numerical estimates for those comparisons are not present in the available abstract. The reported result therefore identifies aerobic vaginitis as the condition with the highest recurrence rate in this subgroup, rather than demonstrating that it caused HPV persistence. Because the design was retrospective and observational, the findings are subject to several constraints. The results describe a single hospital population in Guangzhou and may not apply to women with cervical low-grade lesions treated elsewhere or to people with different HPV subtype distributions. The persistence classification depended on repeated detection of the same high-risk HPV subtype, while the transient category required infection to be present for more than 30 but less than 365 days. The reported models adjust for measured variables, but the available study summary does not specify all potential confounders or establish the completeness of follow-up. The inverse associations involving bacterial vaginosis, intermediate bacterial vaginosis and vulvovaginal candidiasis likewise should not be interpreted as protective effects. Overall, the study offers a hospital-based pattern analysis of viral persistence and recurrent vaginal infection in women with cervical low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, with the largest adjusted associations involving age, HPV-52/58 and multiple high-risk HPV infections. Meeting Coverage > IDWeek Study Supports Starting HPV Vaccination at a Younger Age — Kids who started the series at age 9 or 10 years more likely to get both shots by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today October 21, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday WASHINGTON -- Children who started the two-dose human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine series at age 9 or 10 years were more likely to get both shots versus those who began later, a cluster randomized trial showed. Across 31 U.S. pediatric practices, kids who were recommended to receive HPV vaccination starting at age 9 or 10 had better initiation and completion rates by age 13 versus those who received vaccination starting at age 11 or 12: Initiation rates: 77.1% vs 67% (adjusted HR 2.52, 95% CI 1.93-3.27) Completion rates: 61.6% vs 45.1% (aHR 2.85, 95% CI 2.12-3.83) "What our data show is that the age at which families first hear about the HPV vaccine recommendation changes how many children are protected, and how soon," said Sean O'Leary, MD, MPH, of the Children's Hospital Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus in Aurora, during a press briefing ahead of the IDWeekopens in a new tab or window annual meeting. "For clinicians who now start at 11 or older, we would suggest at least considering earlier introduction in their offices." Though safe and highly effective at preventing HPV infection and a range of subsequent HPV-related cancersopens in a new tab or window, vaccine uptake may not be high enoughopens in a new tab or window to deliver herd immunity. Key vaccination guidelines suggest that an earlier start to HPV vaccination is possible, and previous research has shown that a head start can be effectiveopens in a new tab or window. The CDC recommends HPV vaccinationopens in a new tab or window for children at ages 11 or 12 years, though the agency notes that vaccination can start at age 9. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends starting the vaccine series between 9 and 12 yearsopens in a new tab or window, "at an age that the provider deems optimal for acceptance and completion of the vaccination series." O'Leary noted that his study's results should help shift recommendations toward stronger endorsements of an earlier starting age. "We would suggest that policymakers consider a preferential recommendation for starting at ages 9 or 10, rather than simply permitting it," he said. The trial randomized 31 pediatric practices in California and Colorado from 2021 to 2026 to either introduce the HPV vaccine at ages 9 or 10 (16 practices) or to continue recommending a start at ages 11 or 12 (15 practices). All practices received online training on recommending HPV vaccination, as well as annual booster training and practice-level data reviews. The early-start clinics also received guidance on talking with parents about starting HPV vaccination earlier. "That's important, because we tested the timing of the change by itself -- not a package of interventions," O'Leary noted. The trial included 62,271 children and adolescents ages 9 to 13 years. Nearly half (48.5%) were female, and roughly 22% were on Medicaid. Getting an earlier start at age 9 didn't affect receipt of other vaccines or later well-child visits, "which was one of the concerns going into this study," O'Leary noted. Rates of well-child visits at 11 or 12 years didn't differ between the two groups, nor did meningococcal or tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap) vaccination rates by age 13. Parental hesitancy and acceptance also didn't differ much between the groups. The main pushback in the early-start group came from parents who didn't realize a shot would happen at the well visit and had told their children there wouldn't be shots, O'Leary said. There are practical reasons why getting a head start on HPV vaccination may work better, he explained. The 9-year-old wellness visit is less crowded from a vaccine standpoint than the multiple-vaccine visit at age 11 or 12. Earlier HPV vaccination also may allow clinicians to more effectively frame the vaccine as cancer prevention, he added, rather than as a conversation about sexual health. Research also shows that vaccination at younger ages still leads to longer-term protection. "What we've seen is there doesn't appear to be any waning of protection," O'Leary said. "It's really a remarkable vaccine in that sense." Please enable JavaScript to view the comments powered by Disqus. Waters Corporation and Quest Diagnostics Help Close Cervical Cancer Screening Gap Bringing Nationwide Access to the Most Comprehensive FDA-Cleared At-Home HPV Screening Option PR Newswire Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:00 AM EDT 8 min read DGX -0.57% WAT -0.42% Expands access to most comprehensive FDA-approved HPV test and at-home self-collection option across Quest's national clinician, health plan, and consumer channels starting in 2027 First and only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all ASCCP Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines by providing comprehensive extended genotyping Quest Diagnostics serves half of U.S. physicians and hospitals and one in three American adults each year MILFORD, Mass. and SECAUCUS, N.J., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Quest Diagnostics (NYSE: DGX), a leader in diagnostic information services, and Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT), a global life sciences and diagnostics leader, today announced a collaboration intended to broaden access to clinically appropriate at-home cervical cancer screening through the FDA-cleared OnclarityTM Self-Collection Kit.1,2,13 This collaboration is the first formed by Waters that will provide access to the Onclarity Self-Collection Kit through clinical, health plan, and consumer health channels, along with patient service centers, in the United States. Quest serves one in three American adults and one in two physicians and hospitals each year, and has a nationwide network of over 2,000 patient service centers. This marks a significant step forward in the fight against cervical cancer, positioning both companies at the forefront of closing the U.S. screening gap. Cervical cancer is largely preventable with regular screening and early detection of human papillomavirus (HPV), the leading cause of cervical cancer, yet screening gaps persist, in part because of the sample collection process of traditional tests, which is often inaccessible and uncomfortable for patients.2-6 The Onclarity Self-Collection Kit used with the BD OnclarityTM HPV Assay delivers breakthrough innovation by offering at-home patient self-collection while simultaneously reporting an extended number of individual HPV genotypes to provide more comprehensive results.7,14 "In the U.S., there are over 24 million un- and under-screened individuals and approximately 14,000 new cases of cervical cancer each year," 8 said Jeff Andrews, M.D., FRCSC, Vice President of Medical Affairs, Waters Advanced Diagnostics, Waters Corporation. "By bringing together Waters' diagnostic innovation with Quest's national reach and capabilities, we have an opportunity to make a meaningful impact for these millions of individuals who remain at risk, advancing our shared goal of eliminating this highly preventable disease." Story Continues Beginning in 2027, Quest will drive expanded patient access to Waters' innovation through their broad clinician channel, their Gaps in Care channel serving health insurance plans, and their consumer-initiated testing channel, questhealth.com, all combined with access to their patient service center network. "Many women struggle to participate in traditional cervical cancer screening methods, primarily due to geographic, socioeconomic, and logistical barriers," said board-certified OB/GYN Damian ("Pat") Alagia, M.D., Senior Medical Director, Women's & Reproductive Health, Quest Diagnostics. "We believe in making healthcare more proactive, personal, and connected for all patients, including through transformational options like at-home self-collection to help fill critical gaps in access to care." With the new self-collection option, more patients will be able to collect their own sample in the comfort of their home using the Onclarity Self-Collection Kit, enabled by the BD Onclarity HPV Assay.7 Patients will then mail the sample back to Quest or drop it off at one of the approximately 2,000 Quest patient service centers nationwide. Quest's full-service laboratory will process samples, powered by the fully automated BD CORTM System, which uses advanced robotics to prepare, analyze, and report results while preserving specimen integrity and ensuring reliable, high-quality outcomes.9 Certain HPV genotypes, including types 16, 18, and 45, are associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, making genotype-specific information important for patient management.10 As HPV vaccination has reduced infections from HPV types 16 and 18, other high-risk HPV strains now account for a growing share of cervical disease, particularly among younger, vaccinated populations.11 The Onclarity Self-Collection Kit is enabled by the BD Onclarity HPV Assay, the first and only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all of the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines.7,10 Updated Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) guidelines identify high-risk HPV testing, whether clinician- or self-collected, as the preferred screening method for average-risk individuals ages 30 to 65.12 The BD Onclarity HPV Assay offers extended genotyping beyond HPV 16, 18, and 45 and individually identifies HPV types 16, 18, 31, 45, 51, and 52 along with three sets of strategically pooled results, regardless of collection method.7 Quest Diagnostics is a leader in women's and reproductive health and offers a complete menu of solutions for screening and diagnosing cervical cancer. For more information, visit www.QuestWomensHealth.com. Waters Corporation is an advanced diagnostics leader, offering the FDA-cleared Onclarity HPV Self-Collection Kit for at-home use, used with the BD Onclarity HPV Assay with extended genotyping, marking a significant milestone in expanding access to cervical cancer screening and removing barriers that currently prevent many individuals from receiving routine screening. About Quest Diagnostics: Quest Diagnostics works across healthcare to create a healthier world, one life at a time. We connect people, from clinicians to consumers, with laboratory insights that illuminate a path to better health. With a focus on delivering smarter, simpler testing, we help reveal new avenues to identify and treat disease, empower healthy behaviors, and improve healthcare management. Quest Diagnostics serves half the physicians and hospitals in the United States and one in three American adults each year, and our nearly 60,000 employees work together to deliver diagnostic insights that inspire actions to transform lives. www.QuestDiagnostics.com About Waters Corporation: Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT) is a global leader in life sciences and diagnostics, dedicated to accelerating the benefits of pioneering science through analytical technologies, informatics, and service. With a focus on regulated, high-volume testing environments, our innovative portfolio harnesses deep scientific expertise across chemistry, physics, and biology. We collaborate with customers around the world to advance the release of effective, high-quality medicines, ensure the safety of food and water, and drive better patient outcomes by detecting diseases earlier, managing routine infections, and combating antibiotic resistance. Through a shared culture of relentless innovation, our passionate team of ~15,000 colleagues turn scientific challenges into breakthroughs that improve lives worldwide. Children starting at ages 9–10 achieved significantly higher completion rates (aHR: 2.85; 95% CI: 2.12–3.83). Early initiation circumvents adolescent vaccine fatigue and avoids stigma around sexual health discussions. INITIATING pediatric HPV vaccination at ages 9–10 significantly accelerates adolescent series completion rates before age thirteen. New findings from a cluster randomized controlled trial presented at IDWeek 2026 demonstrate that lowering the starting age of human papillomavirus vaccination from the traditional 11–12 year window yields substantial long-term gains in immunizing adolescents against oncogenic infections. Clinical Benefits of Early HPV Vaccine Initiation Conducted across 31 pediatric practices in Colorado and California between 2021 and 2026, the trial evaluated 16 clinics randomized to introduce the vaccine at ages 9–10 alongside 15 clinics maintaining standard initiation at ages 11–12. All participating clinicians underwent structured online training, practice-based workflow optimization, and annual booster sessions. Baseline practice characteristics, patient volume, and Medicaid proportions were evenly balanced between the two cohorts. Adolescents in practices initiating vaccination at ages 9–10 achieved markedly superior clinical coverage. By age 13, 77.1% of patients in the early cohort initiated the series and 61.6% completed all recommended doses. In contrast, clinics introducing the HPV vaccine at ages 11–12 achieved 67.0% initiation and only 45.1% completion. Early HPV vaccine initiation yielded an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.52 for series initiation and 2.85 for series completion, confirming that earlier administration secures durable protection rather than merely shifting immunization timing. Overcoming Implementation Barriers in Primary Care Approximately 13 million individuals in the United States acquire human papillomavirus annually, predisposing unvaccinated adolescents to anogenital, oropharyngeal, and cervical cancer. Although the Food and Drug Administration approved nine-valent vaccination starting at age 9, national coverage remains suboptimal, leaving approximately 37% of adolescents inadequately protected. While current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends routine vaccination at ages 11 or 12, the American Academy of Pediatrics endorses starting between ages 9 and 12. Adolescent visits at ages 11–12 often present clinical obstacles, including scheduling congestion from multiple mandated school immunizations and provider discomfort with sexual health discussions. Starting HPV vaccine initiation at ages 9–10 establishes a proactive pathway that uncouples cancer vaccines from routine adolescent bundles, supporting policy changes toward preferential early initiation. Reference O’Leary S et al. Impact of switching human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine initiation to ages 9-10 on vaccination coverage: Results of a cluster randomized controlled trial. Oral Abstract 89. While current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends routine vaccination at ages 11 or 12, the American Academy of Pediatrics endorses starting between ages 9 and 12. Adolescent visits at ages 11–12 often present clinical obstacles, including scheduling congestion from multiple mandated school immunizations and provider discomfort with sexual health discussions. Starting HPV vaccine initiation at ages 9–10 establishes a proactive pathway that uncouples cancer vaccines from routine adolescent bundles, supporting policy changes toward preferential early initiation. Reference. O’Leary S et al. Impact of switching human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine initiation to ages 9-10 on vaccination coverage: Results of a cluster randomized controlled trial. Oral Abstract 89. The HPV vaccine reduces the likelihood of getting infected with the main cancer-causing types of HPV (ETV Bharat) By ETV Bharat Health Team Published : October 19, 2026 at 2:44 PM IST 3 Min Read Cervical cancer develops slowly, often following a persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV). During this time the cells of the cervix can change in an abnormal way and not have any obvious symptoms. So, even women who are feeling healthy and have no gynecological complaints should have a cervical screening, according to Dr. Rashmika Gandhi, Fertility Specialist, Birla Fertility & IVF, Gurgaon Sector 14. How Does HPV Testing Differ From Pap Tests? HPV is a common virus that is spread mainly through skin-to-skin contact. Most infections are cleared by the immune system of the body. But some high-risk types can stay around, leading to precancerous changes that can develop into cervical cancer if they are not detected and treated. However, a woman having an HPV infection does not mean she has or will get cancer, clarifies Dr. Gandhi. Both tests can help prevent cervical cancer, but they look at different things: HPV test: Tests for high-risk HPV types that can lead to cervical cancer. Pap smear: Checks for abnormal cervical cells that could be precancerous. Depending on screening protocol, age and medical history, a woman might be advised to have an HPV test and/or a Pap test. These tests are generally recommended every three to five years. “Women should talk to their gynecologist about their screening schedule, rather than wait for symptoms to develop,” says Dr. Gandhi. Why Is Regular Screening Important? The development of precancerous lesions and their progression to cervical cancer is a long process. This allows for regular screening to detect abnormal changes and to take action before it develops into cancer. Finding and treating precancerous lesions can reduce the chance of getting cervical cancer. But What If The Result Is Abnormal? “An abnormal Pap result does not mean cancer, and a positive high-risk HPV test does not mean that there are precancerous changes. Depending on the results, the next step for evaluation is determined. Results may include the reported HPV type and the degree of abnormality,” says Dr. Gandhi. If indicated, a doctor may recommend repeat testing, colposcopy (examination of the cervix under magnification) or biopsy. Regular follow-up is important as precancerous lesions can be detected and treated before they become cancer. Can Cervical Cancer Be Prevented? The HPV vaccine reduces the likelihood of getting infected with the main cancer-causing types of HPV. HPV vaccines can be given to people between the ages of 11 and 45 years. The best time to be vaccinated is before first sexual contact, which will give protection before any possible contact with the virus. Vaccination does not eliminate the need for cervical screening, however. Dr. Gandhi says that women should also get medical evaluation for bleeding after intercourse, bleeding between periods, or persistent unusual vaginal discharge. These symptoms have multiple potential etiologies and should not be assessed solely based on routine screening. Cervical cancer prevention includes vaccination, screening, and timely follow-up. They each do something different, and none are a substitute for the others. Also read: Pune-based Lab Launches HPV Self-Sampling Kit To Make Cervical Cancer Testing More Accessible One Shot Or Two? content_title: Waters and Labcorp to Expand Access to Cervical Cancer Screening with the Most Comprehensive FDA-Approved HPV Testing Option Beginning in Late 2026
content: Labcorp intends to be the first commercial laboratory to offer FDA-approved HPV testing with the BD OnclarityTM HPV Assay across clinician-collected and self-collected screening options in clinic, patient service center, and at-home settings Through a network serving more than 850,000 physicians and healthcare providers and more than 2,200 patient service centers, Labcorp is helping expand access to cervical cancer screening nationwide First and only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all ASCCP Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines by providing comprehensive extended genotyping MILFORD, Mass. and BURLINGTON, N.C., Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Labcorp (NYSE: LH), a global leader of innovative and comprehensive laboratory services, and Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT), a global life sciences and diagnostics leader, today announced a partnership to expand access to the FDA-approved BD Onclarity HPV Assay through Labcorp's nationwide laboratory network beginning in late 2026. Cervical cancer is largely preventable through routine screening and early detection of human papillomavirus (HPV), yet millions of women remain overdue for recommended tests. This collaboration is designed to help address persistent cervical cancer screening gaps by bringing more accessible screening options to patients across the United States. Labcorp will provide these HPV testing options to support its clinician programs, Gaps in Care health plan programs, and Labcorp OnDemand consumer channel.2-8 "Barriers such as privacy, access, and socioeconomic factors can make it difficult to stay current with cervical cancer screening," said Jeff Andrews, M.D., FRCSC, Vice President of Medical Affairs, Waters Advanced Diagnostics, Waters Corporation.5-7 "We are at the start of a new era in which screening can extend beyond the clinic, enable more personalized risk assessment, and reach people who have historically been underserved. By offering greater flexibility in how and where people are screened, our collaboration marks a critical step forward in bridging one of today's most profound care gaps." The Most Comprehensive FDA-Approved HPV Testing Option The BD Onclarity HPV Assay is the only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines.2,9 "Cervical cancer screening saves lives, but too many women still face barriers to getting screened," said Dr. Brian Caveney, Chief Medical and Scientific Officer, Labcorp. "By expanding access and options for comprehensive FDA-approved HPV testing, we can help more women stay current with recommended screening, reach those who may be overdue for care, and support earlier identification of cervical cancer risk." Certain HPV genotypes, including types 16, 18 and 45, are associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, making genotype-specific information important for patient management.9 As HPV vaccination has reduced infections from HPV types 16 and 18, other high-risk HPV strains now account for a growing share of cervical disease, particularly among younger, vaccinated populations.10 The BD Onclarity HPV Assay offers extended genotyping that individually identifies HPV types 16, 18, 31, 45, 51 and 52 along with three sets of strategically pooled results, regardless of collection method, making it the most comprehensive HPV screening tool available in the U.S. today.2,11 Waters and Labcorp intend to offer the BD Onclarity HPV Assay by the end of 2026. To learn more, visit https://womenshealth.labcorp.com/providers/cervical-cancer-screening . About Labcorp: Labcorp (NYSE: LH) is a global leader of innovative and comprehensive laboratory services that helps doctors, hospitals, pharmaceutical companies, researchers and patients make clear and confident decisions. We provide insights and advance science to improve health and improve lives through our unparalleled diagnostics and drug development laboratory capabilities. The company's nearly 71,000 employees serve clients in approximately 100 countries, provided support for more than 85% of the new drugs and therapeutic products approved by the FDA in 2025 and performed more than 750 million tests for patients around the world. Learn more at www.labcorp.com About Waters Corporation: Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT) is a global leader in life sciences and diagnostics, dedicated to accelerating the benefits of pioneering science through analytical technologies, informatics, and service. With a focus on regulated, high-volume testing environments, our innovative portfolio harnesses deep scientific expertise across chemistry, physics, and biology. We collaborate with customers around the world to advance the release of effective, high-quality medicines, ensure the safety of food and water, and drive better patient outcomes by detecting diseases earlier, managing routine infections, and combating antibiotic resistance. Through a shared culture of relentless innovation, our passionate team of ~15,000 colleagues turn scientific challenges into breakthroughs that improve lives worldwide. For more information, please visit www.waters.com/about . Disclaimer: The BD Biosciences and BD Diagnostic Solutions businesses have been acquired by Waters Corporation ("Waters"). Becton, Dickinson and Company or one of its affiliates or subsidiaries ("BD") remains the legal manufacturer of Biosciences and Diagnostic Solutions products until all required regulatory transfers are completed. During this interim period, BD maintains full responsibility for all regulatory obligations of the legal manufacturer. Product information provided here is supplied under BD's regulatory authority. To learn more about the relationship between Waters and BD during this transition period, please see our detailed summary: www.waters.com/bdtransaction . BD is a trademark of Becton, Dickinson and Company. Waters is a trademark of Waters Corporation or its affiliates. All other marks are the property of their respective owners. The BD Onclarity HPV Assay is manufactured by Becton, Dickinson and Company or one of its affiliates or subsidiaries. Each of the forward-looking statements is subject to change based on various important factors, many of which are beyond the control of Labcorp or Waters Corporation. These factors, in some cases, have affected and in the future (together with other factors) could affect the ability of Labcorp or Waters Corporation to implement its respective business strategy, and actual results could differ materially from those suggested by these forward-looking statements. As a result, readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on any of the forward-looking statements. The forward-looking statements included in this release represent the companies' estimates or views as of the date of this release and should not be relied upon as representing the companies' estimates or views as of any date subsequent to the date of this release. Neither Labcorp nor Waters Corporation has any obligation to provide any updates to these forward-looking statements even if its expectations change. Reasons young men are unwilling to be vaccinated include concerns about the cost and number of doses, as well as a lack of awareness. The study pointed out that among unvaccinated men, more than 90 per cent said they were willing to pay up to S$250 for the vaccine. Another nearly one-fifth said they would get vaccinated only if it was free. Experts believe vaccination rates among men may rise after the HPV9 vaccine is added next year to the National Adult Immunisation Schedule and the list of subsidised vaccines. Read More 本地一项研究发现,未接种人乳头瘤病毒(Human Papillomavirus,HPV)疫苗的年轻男性中,有四分之三对接种疫苗持开放态度,但实际接种率只有约一成。 研究显示,年轻男性不愿接种的原因包括,对接种费用、接种次数有所顾虑,以及认识不足。 这项研究由新加坡保健服务集团综合诊疗所(SingHealth Polyclinics)旗下的基层医疗研究所(Primary Care Research Institute)领导,并与杜克-新加坡国立大学医学院及华侨中学的科学研究与人才培育中心(CenTaD)合作开展。 共有590名年龄介于15岁到24岁的国人参与调查。其中,男性占四成,女性占六成。 根据新保集团发布的文告,约80%的受访女性已经接种了人乳头瘤病毒疫苗,男性的接种率则只有11%,明显低很多。 不过,在还没接种疫苗的受访者当中,男女的接种意愿都偏高。近73%的男性和79%的女性表示,有意接种这个疫苗。 文告指出,七成的子宫颈癌病例是由人乳头瘤病毒引起。不过,这个病毒也可能引发其他癌症和生殖器疣(genital warts),而且男女都可能感染。 然而,男性对这个病毒的认识仍然不足。近八成的受访男性知道它可感染女性,却有超过一半的人不知道,男性也同样可能感染。 对于接种疫苗带来的益处,不论男女,只有约五分之一的受访者了解,疫苗有助于降低男性患生殖器疣和肛门癌的风险。另外,只有约三分之一的受访者知道,男性也可以接种这个疫苗。 CONTENT CONTINUES AFTER THIS ADVERTISEMENT 明年新措施或可助提高男性接种率 新保集团综合诊疗所数据科学与研究部高级分析师、同时也是这项研究的主要作者Ng Ding Xuan表示,研究发现,表明男性不接种疫苗的主要原因不在“污名”,而是对费用、便利性和潜在副作用的顾虑。因此,男性接种率可通过一些措施来改善。 “研究结果表明,如果能让疫苗接种变得更可负担、更容易获取和更便利,年轻男性的疫苗接种率将有机会提高。” 研究也发现,在未接种疫苗的男性当中,超过九成表示愿意支付最高250元来接种疫苗。另有近五分之一的男性表示,只有在疫苗免费的情况下才愿意接种。 政府这个月初宣布,明年1月1日起,九价人乳头瘤病毒(HPV9)疫苗将纳入全国成人免疫计划(National Adult Immunisation Schedule)和受津贴疫苗清单(Subsidised Vaccine List)。专家认为,新措施有望提高男性接种率。 另外,研究显示,超过半数的受访者主要是通过学校的宣传活动,获取有关人乳头瘤的信息。 由此看来,善用学校和数码平台来向年轻男性传达关于人乳头瘤、疫苗接种及可预防疾病的更明确信息,相信能发挥作用。 相关报道: HPV9疫苗明年起 将纳入全国免疫计划 新加坡 02/10/2026 18:28 HPV9疫苗明年起 将纳入全国免疫计划 相关标签 人类乳头状瘤病毒 HPV 疫苗 新加坡保健集团 SingHealth 订阅电邮简报 每日接收头条新闻内容 Subscribe now 下载《8视界》应用程序 一机在手,掌握天下事 Download App 加入Telegram群组 天天送上精选好内容! content: newsinfo / Nation Nation DOH eyes HPV vaccination for over 2 million girls nationwide By: Dianne Sampang - @inquirerdotnet INQUIRER.net / 08:53 PM October 19, 2026 Mayor Chrislyn Abadilla of Banna, Ilocos Norte, a physician, administers an HPV vaccine to a 9-year-old schoolgirl on May 10, 2024. Banna became the first local government unit in the country to achieve 90-percent vaccination coverage among girls aged 9 to 14 in the fight against cervical cancer. Photo from Disease Prevention and Control Section, DOH-CHD Ilocos. MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday said it is eyeing to vaccinate over 2 million girls in Grades 4 and 5 nationwide against human papillomavirus (HPV) under its school immunization program. According to Dr. Alethea De Guzman, director of the DOH Epidemiology Bureau, the agency recommends a single dose of the vaccine for females aged 9 to 14, as this is the most effective period for vaccination before possible exposure to the virus. READ: DOH steps up drive to address low vaccination coverage, hesitancy Article continues after this advertisement “According to DPCV, we are eyeing to vaccinate 2.007 million learners from grades 4 and 5 from public and private schools against HPV for our Bakuna Eskwela,” De Guzman said during a media briefing. Cayetano She also said out-of-school youth can avail of the vaccines at the nearest health centers. “Of the approximately 2 million learners, around 9 percent are out-of-school youth,” she added. When asked about the DOH’s latest data on cervical cancer in the country, De Guzman explained that the illness is not a disease under surveillance, for which the agency can typically collect data every month. READ: DOH starts early procurement of vaccines for 2027 immunization Article continues after this advertisement She also said the Philippine Cancer Institute had already begun its hospital-based cancer registry to facilitate more timely collection of information. Citing the International Agency for Research on Cancer, she said there were 7,829 cervical cancer patients in the Philippines as of 2024. Article continues after this advertisement De Guzman also underscored the importance of school immunization programs, such as HPV vaccination, in raising awareness of cervical cancer, which she noted is the second-leading cause of cancer in the country. “Sometimes, when we talk about cervical cancer, we immediately discuss screening, chemotherapy, and remedies. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Tongan adults highlight vaccine trust and HPV awareness gaps by October 22, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Tongan adults highlight vaccine trust and HPV awareness gaps Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A qualitative pilot study of 19 Tongan adults in Utah found that most participants were unaware of the human papillomavirus vaccine, while attitudes toward vaccination varied by age, social network and access to culturally relevant health information. Fifteen of the 19 participants, or 78.9%, lacked awareness of the HPV vaccine and its role in preventing cervical cancer, according to the study published in BMC Public Health. The findings come amid documented inequities in routine vaccination among Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander communities in the United States, a group that also faces a higher risk of death from HPV-related cervical cancer than other populations. The researchers said broad category labels can obscure cultural, social and linguistic differences within those communities, including the experiences of Tongans. The researchers conducted three focus group discussions in February and March 2024 with Tongan adults aged 18 and older who lived in Utah. Groups were conducted in English and Tongan. The study used the Socioecological Model and Social Cognitive Theory to examine behavioral, social and cultural influences on general vaccine attitudes and HPV literacy, experience and access. Discover more vaccine Vaccine Find Vaccines Book a Checkup health Participants showed a generational pattern in where they preferred to obtain vaccine information. Those younger than 55 relied mainly on social media, whereas participants aged 56 to 65 and older expressed greater confidence in healthcare providers. The older group emphasized the importance of trust between patients and physicians, identifying that relationship as central to confidence in vaccination decisions. Within families and households, participants described conformity with traditional gender expectations as a major influence. Tongan women were viewed as the primary caregivers and health decision-makers, with much of the responsibility for household health decisions, including vaccination, assigned to them. The study therefore identified gender and family roles as important parts of the environment in which vaccine acceptance and refusal were considered. Vaccine hesitancy within close social circles was strongly influenced by misinformation, according to the participants. Their accounts also highlighted the strong reliance on traditional medicine and religious leaders in Tongan communities. At the same time, participants said discussions of sexual health and sexually transmitted diseases are constrained by social stigma. The findings indicate that misinformation and culturally influential sources operate alongside limited discussion of subjects directly relevant to HPV vaccination. At the societal level, participants identified several structural barriers: inadequate insurance coverage for preventive and therapeutic services, limited access to health information in culturally and linguistically appropriate forms, and under-representation of Tongans among healthcare providers and staff. These gaps were described not only as problems of individual knowledge but also as conditions affecting whether useful information and services could be reached and trusted. Discover more Health Get Health Tips See an OB-GYN Find Cancer Care Browse Reference As a qualitative pilot study, the research was designed to explore experiences and perceptions rather than estimate vaccination rates or test an intervention. Its sample was small and geographically limited to Tongan adults in Utah, and the findings arose from three facilitated discussions conducted in two languages. The authors said the results underscore the need for culturally specific and culturally humble vaccine messaging and strategies at multiple social-ecological levels, particularly to address misinformation and barriers affecting HPV vaccine awareness and acceptance. Subject of Research: Tongan adults’ vaccine attitudes, HPV awareness and access barriers in Utah Article Title: Navigating vaccine beliefs: a qualitative pilot study of general vaccine attitudes and HPV awareness among Tongan adults Article References: Obray, A. M., Skyles, T. J., Poole, B. D., Bashford, T. M., Hoelzer, H., Davis, S. C., Petersen, L. G., Fox, D., Sloan, D. S., Vergara, M. A. C., & Novilla, M. L. B. (2026). Navigating vaccine beliefs: a qualitative pilot study of general vaccine attitudes and HPV awareness among Tongan adults. Send Close Pediatric Infections Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print OCTOBER 21, 2026 IDWeek 2026 Starting HPV Vaccine at Age 9 or 10 Raises Series Completion by 13 By Gina Shaw Moving the start of the HPV vaccine series from 11 to 12 years of age to ages 9 to 10 substantially increased the share of children who began and finished the series by their 13th birthday, according to a cluster randomized trial to be presented at IDWeek 2026, in Washington, D.C. (abstract 89). Source: Adobe. “The age at which families first hear the recommendation changes how many children are protected and how soon,” said lead author Sean O’Leary, MD, MPH, a professor of pediatrics and infectious diseases at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Children’s Hospital Colorado, in Aurora, during an Infectious Diseases Society of America press briefing on Oct. 15. Related Content Measles Resurgence and a Vaccine Guidance Vacuum Complicate Back-to-School Season The United States is facing its worst measles resurgence in more than three decades at a moment when no federal ... New Interactive Tool Compares Vaccine Versus Disease Risk “What’s the Risk?” is a new interactive online tool aimed at helping doctors and patients better ... Global Rubella Elimination Progress Continues Substantial progress has been made toward global rubella and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) elimination, but ... HPV vaccine uptake in the United States has stalled, Dr. O’Leary noted. “The CDC’s 2025 National Immunization Survey found that 63% of teens aged 13 to 17 were up to date, and that marks several years in a row without a significant increase. Among 13-year-olds, fewer than half were up to date.” Federal guidance recommends routine vaccination at 11 or 12 years and permits starting at age 9. Observational studies have linked earlier initiation to better on-time completion but could not establish cause and effect (Hum Vaccin Immunother 2023;19[1]:2180971). The National Cancer Institute–funded trial randomized 31 pediatric practices in Colorado and California that had been starting HPV vaccination at 11 to 12 years. From 2021 to 2026, 16 practices switched to starting at 9 to 10 years and 15 continued at 11 to 12. Both arms received training on recommending the vaccine and annual feedback on missed opportunities. The trial included more than 62,000 children. In the early-start practices, the median age at series completion was 12.2 years, compared with 13.3 years in the comparison practices, and the median age at initiation was 11.0 versus 11.8 years. By age 13, 61.7% versus 45.1% of children had completed the series, and 77.2% versus 67.0% had initiated it. After adjustment, children in the early-start practices were more than twice as likely to start and complete the series. “That’s 16.6 percentage points more children protected, or 37% more children,” Dr. O’Leary said. The effect held in both Colorado and California. The investigators found no evidence of harm. Rates of well-child visits at 11 to 12 years did not differ between arms, nor did Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis) or meningococcal vaccination by age 13. “Starting early didn’t crowd out the other adolescent vaccines, which was one of the concerns going into this study,” Dr. O’Leary said. Parental hesitancy did not appear to differ between groups. The 11- to 12-year visit is crowded with other vaccines, Dr. O’Leary noted. “If one of those is skipped, it’s usually the HPV vaccine, and many of those adolescents never end up getting it, leaving them at risk for a preventable cancer,” he said. Starting earlier may also help frame the vaccine as cancer prevention rather than a conversation about sexuality, he added. “For clinicians who now start at 11 or older, we would suggest at least considering earlier introduction in their offices,” Dr. O’Leary said. “We would also suggest that policymakers consider a preferential recommendation for starting at ages 9 or 10, rather than simply permitting it.” O’Leary reported no relevant financial disclosures. Mamaga knows best: Togolese queens counsel confidence in vaccination

In Togo, “mamagas” – community matriarchs – support efforts to stem the flow of vaccine misinformation.

  • 23 October 2026
  • by Olivier Konan

Vaccination anxiety seemed to be mounting in Togo’s capital, Lomé, as rumours amplified on social media during the COVID-19 pandemic fuelled doubt among families.

Across the city, Mamagas – the wives of the canton chiefs – were hearing the same concerns from parents, again and again. If a child developed a fever or swelling after vaccination, parents worried that something had gone wrong. Without adequate information, mild and expected reactions seemed to some like signs that the vaccine was unsafe.

Some parents stopped taking their children to health centres entirely. Others refused to open their doors to health workers. The cervical cancer-preventing human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine had been introduced to Togo’s immunisation schedule in 2023 and was proving to be a particular focus for public worry.

During the meetings organised for women, the Mamaga spoke with my mother, who then spoke with my father, and ultimately they decided together that I should be vaccinated.

- Aka Isabela, now protected against HPV

But coverage with far more familiar antigens was dipping too: in 2025, just 13% of the eligible children of Greater Lomé were properly protected against polio. The Ministry of Health recognised that a new approach was needed to build confidence in vaccination.

“We asked ourselves what was going wrong,” says Kamna Nana Tena, Head of the Communication Section at the Immunisation Division, which implements the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI). Following a recommendation from the civil society organisation known as the Platform for Vaccination and Immunisation (POSCVI), they decided to turn to a trusted source of influence within communities: the Mamagas.

Turning to trusted voices

Although Mamagas do not publicly participate in community council meetings, they play a central role in community life.

“The Matriarch has the chief’s ear,” explains Niba Lobo, Mamaga of the Badja community. She explains that the chief may pause discussions to seek her advice privately, and community members turn to the Mamaga for “mediation in marital matters, support for mothers and child protection”.

Mamagas come from diverse backgrounds. “Some are civil servants or leaders of women’s associations. Others are traders, hairdressers, seamstresses or homemakers,” explains As Attiso Afansi épouse Dravie, Mamaga of the Anyrokopé community.

This diverse group of women have something important in common – they have the trust of their communities.

A new network for vaccination

POSCVI began by mapping the Mamagas across the region, to identify those whose influence and legitimacy were deeply anchored in their communities. The organisation then established a local Mamaga network, giving these leaders a shared structure and a collective voice.

“The network then designated focal points in each compound, ensuring that every community had a direct link to the campaign,” explains Augustin Kola, Coordinator of the Gavi CHA project in Togo.

Since 2025, POSCVI has built its awareness raising with the help of the Mamagas – they are co-creators, not just messengers.

Together with POSCVI, they design every message, shape every outreach effort, and carry the voice of vaccination into communities – from routine immunisation efforts to the HPV vaccine. This approach turned campaigns into a shared commitment that communities trust and embrace.

To equip them for this role, POSCVI, supported by the EPI and Health Promotion staff, trained Mamagas on three key skills: how to identify rumours circulating in their communities, how to respond with fact-based information adapted to the audience, and how to explain, in simple terms, the normal side-effects of the HPV vaccine, including pain at the injection site and brief, mild discomfort.

The goal was not simply to provide information – it was to make that information understandable, relevant and reassuring.

One conversation at a time

With POSCVI’s coordination, the Mamagas used three complementary approaches to meet the communities where they already gathered. They held educational discussions in markets, places of worship and women’s groups. They conducted home visits to engage directly with hesitant families, and they mobilised community and religious leaders to publicly support vaccination.

For teenaged student Aka Isabela, these conversations made all the difference. Although she knew that the HPV vaccine was free, she initially followed her mother’s advice to not receive it. The turning point came from the Matriarchs: “During the meetings organised for women, the Mamaga spoke with my mother, who then spoke with my father, and ultimately they decided together that I should be vaccinated,” says Isabela.

A mother could never want her daughter to suffer. Seeing the mothers [Mamagas] at the forefront of the vaccination campaign convinced me to have my son vaccinated against polio. I even encouraged my neighbour, who has a daughter, to have her vaccinated against HPV.

- Agbavon Genevieve, Trader

Mamaga Horafemenusui Kékéli Épse Aklassou is from the Bè canton. For her, personal dialogue and trust-building were crucial after they were notified that the first round of the vaccination campaign had achieved lower-than-expected participation.

“Based on the trust they have in us, we took it upon ourselves to explain to our mothers and sisters why immunisation is important. The second round was a success,” she says.

Have you read?

  • In Brazzaville, Congo, a trusted midwife steps up to offer immunisation to an under-protected district
  • How a cup of tea and an open conversation helped marginalised children get vaccinated in Mauritania

A turning of the tide

This approach produced measurable results. Across the 20 targeted districts, as a result of the combined efforts of POSCVI and the Mamagas, 3,765 children who had been lost to follow-up were found and vaccinated. In addition, 295 zero-dose children who had never received a vaccine before received immune protection.

The impact of the work was also evident in changing attitudes.

“A mother could never want her daughter to suffer. Seeing the mothers [Mamagas] at the forefront of the vaccination campaign convinced me to have my son vaccinated against polio. I even encouraged my neighbour, who has a daughter, to have her vaccinated against HPV,” says Agbavon Genevieve, a trader from Togblé Kopé in Lomé.

Together, POSCVI and the matriarchs have formalised their partnership through a charter of commitment that sets out their shared responsibilities and mutual accountability.

For POSCVI, the experience demonstrates the value of working through existing community structures. Mamagas have shown that building trust in vaccination is not only about sharing accurate information – it is about who delivers this information. By bringing together medical knowledge and traditional legitimacy, the initiative created a bridge between health services and the families they seek to reach.

How is Gavi helping?

With support from Gavi through its Community Health Actors (CHA) project, which ran from January to June 2026, POSCVI worked with EPI and Health Promotion staff to strengthen community trust and uptake of vaccination in Togo.

Active in Togo since 2015, POSCVI brings together 39 local civil society organisations working to strengthen community mobilisation and improve vaccination coverage in the country’s 20 priority districts. Their strategy was simple: to spread health knowledge through the influence and trust that traditional leaders already have within their communities.

Gavi’s CHA project was designed as a strategic initiative to strengthen the role of community actors in identifying and reducing zero-dose children, improving vaccine coverage and institutionalising community health.

Implemented in eight countries in sub-Saharan Africa with operational support from MannionDaniels, the project experimented with innovative indirect financing mechanisms via local civil society organisations (CSOs), domestic resource mobilisation and strengthening existing coordination platforms.
